analysis.one_liner: Bars digital platforms from tracking users without consent and declares personal data the user's property.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced by one representative with no cosponsors, it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for websites and apps to use cookies, tracking pixels, or your personal information without your consent. It would also have declared the information you generate online to be your exclusive property, required platforms to tell you what data they collect and what they think it is worth, and banned platforms from cutting you off if you say no to tracking. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and users themselves could have enforced the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who would gain the right to opt out of tracking, see what platforms think their data is worth, and sue for violations, keeping at least 90 percent of any damages awarded. State attorneys general would gain a new enforcement tool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday internet users and state enforcers

how_it_helps.text: Platforms could not use cookies, collect information about a user's habits or preferences, deliver targeted content, use tracking pixels, or share user information with other platforms without the user's consent [S2].

Any information a user generates on a platform would be treated as an exclusive property right owned by that user, and platforms would have to disclose what they collect, what it will be used for, and what they determine its economic value to be [S2].
Platforms could not restrict a user's access to the platform for declining to consent to tracking, so saying no to cookies could not cost you the service [S2].

Enforcement would have real teeth: FTC penalties, state attorney general lawsuits for penalties and restitution, and a private right of action in which a user keeps at least 90 percent of damages, with attorney fees capped at 33 percent [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Digital platforms, advertising technology companies, data brokers, and the online advertising ecosystem that profits from collecting, selling, and acting on user data without an opt-out.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts any state law relating to its requirements, which could have overridden stronger state privacy protections (such as California's) with a single weaker federal floor [S2].

Its definition of a digital platform is extremely broad — any 'technology-enabled content producer,' covering websites, online businesses, and apps — and treating all collected data as the user's exclusive property is a legal approach no major privacy law uses, raising questions about how basic site functions, analytics, and security practices would comply [S2].

Requiring platforms to assign a dollar value to every user's data and disclose it could create heavy compliance burdens and litigation exposure for small websites and apps, not just large tech firms [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users, the bill offered genuine privacy gains: a real consent requirement, a ban on punishing users who refuse tracking, and meaningful enforcement money going to users rather than governments. The serious design questions are its blanket preemption of state privacy laws and the untested 'data as property' framework, which could have produced confusion or been watered down in practice. It was a serious attempt at consumer protection with significant drafting flaws that a committee process might have addressed — a process it never received.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Schweikert introduced the bill on July 2, 2024 [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action appears in the bill's record [S4].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Digital platforms, advertising technology firms, and data brokers are better off because the bill never moved: the current system of collecting and monetizing user data without an enforceable property right or opt-out remains in place. Internet users gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Digital platforms and the ad-data industry

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 2, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: 435 House members
against.what_they_did: Only the sponsor signed on; no other member of either party cosponsored the bill during its six months of existence.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed; it simply drew no members beyond its author.

industries.note: The bill would ban non-consensual cookies, tracking pixels, and cross-platform data sharing — the core mechanics of behavioral advertising — and require disclosure of the economic value of user data. Its death leaves the targeted-advertising business model untouched.

industries.industry: Data brokers and cross-platform data sharers
industries.note: Sharing information about users with other platforms or online businesses would have required consent, directly cutting into the data resale market.

industries.industry: Websites, apps, and online businesses of all sizes
industries.note: The bill's sweeping definition of 'digital platform' would impose consent, disclosure, and valuation requirements on nearly every site and app, with compliance and litigation costs falling hardest on small operators even as their users gained privacy rights.
